title: From a new tax deadline to a revamped RRSP, six ways the budget could affect your wallet - The Globe and Mail

 Comments Share Save for later Please log in to bookmark this story. Log In Create an account From a new tax deadline and a rethinking of registered retirement savings plans, or RRSPs, to free museum access for children, Prime Minister Mark Carney’s 2026 budget contains a slew of small changes meant to improve Canadians’ personal finances without weighing down the federal purse. 
 A government that has sought out suggestions on tax reform delivered no grand vision for an overhaul of the current system, but has proposed a bevy of tweaks intended to simplify tax filing for both households and businesses. 
 The most notable among them is moving the deadline for filing and paying taxes to May 15, including for self-employed individuals. 
 Ottawa also said it’s considering eliminating the need for Canadians to convert their RRSPs to registered retirement income funds, or RRIFs, in retirement. 
 The budget contains several measures to improve affordability and help lower-income Canadians keep up with the cost of living, including a new boost to the Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit, formerly known as the GST/HST credit. 
 Budget 2026: Ottawa bets spending boost will deliver future economic gains 
 Here are some of the main measures affecting Canadians’ finances: 
 A new tax deadline: Ottawa wants to move the tax deadline, usually set for April 30 for most people, to May 15. The new due date for filing returns and paying taxes would also apply to self-employed individuals, who currently have until June 15 to file. 
 The change will give Canadians and the Canada Revenue Agency more time to tackle tax-season paperwork, something the government said it is hoping will help reduce tax reassessments and the volume of interactions between tax filers and the tax agency. 
 The change would start with the 2028 tax season. 
 No more RRIFs: The government is proposing to merge RRSPs and RRIFs into what it calls a new “RRSP-for-life.” Currently, Canadians can save and invest on a tax-deferred basis inside an RRSP, where their money grows tax-free unless it is withdrawn. But by age 71, they must convert their RRSP into a RRIF, which is meant to help Canadians draw income in retirement and comes with minimum mandatory annual withdrawals that are taxable. 
 Notably, the reform would not change the obligation to make those minimum withdrawals after age 71. Instead, it would simply spare Canadians the paperwork and hassle of converting their account, said Doug Carroll, tax and estate specialist at Aviso Wealth. 
 The government is also weighing changes that would simplify what happens when an RRSP holder dies. Among them is the idea of introducing a “successor holder” designation for RRSPs. 
 This would allow eligible survivors of the account holder, such as a spouse or a common-law partner, to take over the account, as is currently possible for tax-free savings accounts and other registered accounts. 
 Budget 2026 highlights: Tax support for artists, entrepreneurs and billions for new housing 
 Simplified tax filing: The budget contains several measures to reduce tax paperwork for everyday Canadians. 
 Among them, the government proposes to raise the minimum amount of income tax owing that triggers an obligation to pay tax in quarterly instalments throughout the year rather than at tax time. The threshold would increase from $3,000, where it was set in 2008, to $7,500, a level that would be indexed to inflation going forward. In Quebec, where the CRA only collects federal tax, the threshold would rise from $1,800 to $4,500 for individuals. 
 The change would spare the need to pay tax in instalments for self-employed Canadians with modest incomes, as well as seniors who receive modest amounts from sources such as RRIFs, Old Age Security and Canada Pension Plan payments, which are not subject to tax withholding. The new thresholds would apply starting in the 2028 tax year. 
 Also in the spirit of making tax filing easier, the budget proposes to offer Canadians the choice to claim a flat $1,000 per year instead of itemizing their expenses for tax credits and deductions such as the Moving Expense Deduction and the Home Accessibility Tax Credit, which helps homeowners pay for renovations that improve accessibility. 
 “They’re trying to let people get the benefits out of the tax system that are readily available to them without having to keep detailed records,” Mr. Carroll said. 
 Budget 2026: Ottawa plans to merge federal financing agencies, set up standalone sovereign wealth fund 
 A new boost to the Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit: One of the most notable affordability measures in the budget is another increase to the CGEB, which helps lower-income Canadians offset the cost of the GST they pay. 
 The government is proposing a one-time supplement to the benefit equal to half the amount that beneficiaries are eligible for in the current benefit year, which runs until the end of June 2027. The supplement, to be delivered as a one-time payment early next year, will be up to $223 per adult and $117 per child, with a $117 top-up for single adults. 
 Ottawa has already delivered a one-time 50-per-cent benefit supplement in June, followed by a 25-per-cent increase to the regular, quarterly benefit payments that is set to last until 2031. 
 New or beefed-up benefits and tax breaks: Among tweaks to existing credits, the government would turn the Canada Caregiver Credit for Canadians who look after adults with disabilities into a refundable tax credit. This would ensure the financial aid reaches caregivers whose incomes are too low to pay tax. Eligible Canadians could receive up to $1,260 for 2027. 
 Ottawa also proposes lowering the eligibility thresholds and boosting payments for the Canada Workers Benefit, which helps low-income Canadians who have some earnings from work. Recent data collected from food banks across Canada shows that nearly 20 per cent of Canadians who turn to emergency food assistance have at least some income from work. 
 The shored-up benefit, which the government wants to rename Build Canada Workers Benefit, would increase the maximum a single individual can receive from $1,709 to $1,859 a year. Families could receive up to $3,143 annually, an increase from $2,943. 
 The government is also weighing the creation of a non-refundable tax credit for artists, although it said it would announce further details on the measure in its spring fiscal update. 
 Free museum access for children and youth: Among several measures meant to boost cultural initiatives, the budget proposes to make access to national museums free for children and young people under the age of 25. 
 Editor’s note: A previous version of this article incorrectly implied that the value of a deceased person’s RRSP is taxable and added to their final tax return even when a spouse is named as the sole beneficiary. In that scenario, it is possible to transfer the RRSP holdings to the surviving spouse tax-free.
